data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction between truly independent failures and those that merely appear uncorrelated is revealed by the 'Temporal-Dependency Signature': independent failures occur stochastically across the network, while appearing-uncorrelated failures cluster around a latent shared trigger.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The 'shared trigger' is an external event that affects all services regardless of their internal architecture (e.g., a global internet routing collapse).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The failure rate is so high that stochastic independent failures happen to cluster temporally.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Truly independent failures (e.g., hardware bit-rot, local power failure) follow a Poisson distribution over time and space. 'Appearing uncorrelated' failures are actually 'Common Mode Failures' triggered by a shared latent variable (e.g., a leap-second bug, a specific API update). These failures will show a high temporal correlation (happening within a narrow window) or a high dependency correlation (affecting only services sharing a specific library version), even if the services are operationally independent.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
